summary: Asks for information about renumbering experiences, as part of work by the PIER working group to build documents that help sites change their IP addresses. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Moving every computer in an office to a new set of addresses is hard. These folks asked people to share what happened when they did it, so others could learn.

questions: how do sites renumber ip networks
how do sites change ip addresses
what are the challenges of ip renumbering
subtitle: Gathering real-world experiences about changing enterprise network addresses.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, many organizations had to change their IP addresses, a disruptive task with no standard guidance.
tldr.mechanism: The PIER working group asked the Internet community to share real experiences, tools, and lessons learned from renumbering efforts.
tldr.outcome: This memo collects those experiences to help future organizations plan renumbering with fewer surprises.

today: RFC 1916 is informational and is not a standard. It was part of the PIER working group's effort to gather information that would guide future renumbering efforts. As IPv6 adoption eventually occurred, renumbering became less frequent in the classic sense, though the challenges described remain relevant to network operations.

sections.title: Why Renumbering Happens
sections.content:
As the Internet expanded rapidly in the 1990s, many organizations found themselves needing to change the IP addresses of their entire networks. This might happen because they changed Internet service providers, got allocated different address space by a registry, or needed to restructure their addressing plan. Renumbering is technically challenging and disruptive: every router, server, workstation, and application with an embedded IP address must be updated, usually with careful coordination to avoid service interruption.

The PIER working group (Procedures for Internet/Enterprise Renumbering) of the IETF recognized the urgent need for practical guidance and decided to collect real-world experience from organizations that had already renumbered or were in the process.
sections.eli5: When you change address spaces, everything with an old address breaks. Nobody had written down the tricks yet, so the PIER group asked: 'Who's done this? What happened?'

sections.title: What People Needed
sections.content:
Organizations renumbering their networks faced three major challenges. First, identifying what needed to change: not just routers and servers, but configuration files, DNS records, access control lists, license servers, and applications with hardcoded IP addresses. Second, coordinating external updates with ISPs, DNS registries, and other internet registries. Third, managing the human side: notifying staff, handling special cases, and troubleshooting unexpected failures.

The PIER group wanted to collect concrete case studies describing exactly what was done, what worked, what didn't, and what lessons applied to the next renumbering effort.
sections.eli5: It's not just changing one thing—it's finding all the hidden places where addresses are locked in, telling everyone about the change, and fixing problems as they happen.

sections.title: Three Types of Information Sought
sections.content:
The group solicited three categories of information. Renumbering experience: accounts of successful or in-progress efforts, including what was planned, what was done, what went wrong, and lessons for next time. Tool information: descriptions of scripts, software, or hardware tools used to discover what needed changing, generate new configurations, coordinate updates, or verify the results. Application information: lists of specific software or hardware that required special handling—products with hardcoded addresses, vendors no longer in business, or applications needing security key updates.

RFC 1916 emphasized that technical advice was welcome, but so was guidance on managing the human and political dimensions of major network changes.
sections.eli5: They asked for three things: stories of how people did it, tools that helped, and lists of software that caused trouble.

sections.title: Scope and Focus
sections.content:
The working group focused primarily on IPv4 renumbering, not on future protocol changes. The intended audience was single-homed networks not acting as transit providers—the most common case in the 1990s. Organizations renumbering more complex environments, such as multihomed networks or service providers, were encouraged to submit information too, as were accounts of renumbering that was still underway, written as a 'diary' of the actual experience rather than a retrospective.

Submissions could be anonymous if desired, allowing organizations to share sensitive experiences without public identification. The deadline was May 15, 1996, and results were to be published as a series of documents describing processes, available tools, and known problematic applications.
sections.eli5: The focus was on the normal case: offices moving to new addresses. But any real story was welcome, and you could stay anonymous.
